definition: A cusp catastrophe model is a way of describing change that allows outcomes to shift suddenly and non-linearly between two states rather than changing gradually. In this context, it is used to examine how one factor can determine when a sharp jump in distress occurs, while another influences which distress state is more likely.

reasons: The definition’s general characterization (“a way of describing change… between two states rather than changing gradually,” with “suddenly and non-linearly”) is not explicitly stated in the packet text; the packet only notes that the authors tested “self-regulation shift theory” using “cusp catastrophe analyses” to model “non-linear shifts in distress” and “discontinuous symptom acceleration,” without giving a standalone, general definition of the model.

The definition’s phrasing about “when a sharp jump in distress occurs” is not directly stated that way in the packet (the packet describes predicted “non-linear shifts… (i.e., discontinuous symptom acceleration)” and a shift “from a lower state to an upper state,” but does not explicitly frame it as a general “sharp jump” definition of the model).

While the packet supports a mapping to variables labeled as “bifurcation factor” (coping self-efficacy affecting when shifts occur from lower to upper state) and an “asymmetry controlling factor” (loss or peritraumatic dissociation affecting relative strength/likelihood of states), the definition adds extra interpretive wording (“which distress state is more likely”) that is not explicitly expressed in that exact terms in the packet.
